---
title: "Robustness"
---

Two questions about the headline decomposition: does the ranking of the channels
survive a different way of attributing their contributions (Shapley), and does it
survive perturbing the model's key frictions (sensitivity sweeps)?

## Shapley decomposition

The headline marginals activate the channels in a fixed order (U → R → C), which
under-credits whichever channel is added last. The Shapley value averages each
channel's contribution over all six activation orders. Below, canonical (sequential)
against Shapley, for each channel, at four intensities. The sign is the same under both
rules; what changes is the *ranking* — the central-bank channel is systematically
under-credited by the sequential order at moderate stress, and dominates in the tail.

```{ojs}
shap = FileAttachment("../data/shapley_decomp.csv").csv({typed: true})
shapLong = shap.flatMap(r => [
  {intensity: r.intensity, channel: "Unsecured",   rule: "Canonical", value: r.canonical_U},
  {intensity: r.intensity, channel: "Unsecured",   rule: "Shapley",   value: r.shapley_U},
  {intensity: r.intensity, channel: "Repo",        rule: "Canonical", value: r.canonical_R},
  {intensity: r.intensity, channel: "Repo",        rule: "Shapley",   value: r.shapley_R},
  {intensity: r.intensity, channel: "CB credit",   rule: "Canonical", value: r.canonical_C},
  {intensity: r.intensity, channel: "CB credit",   rule: "Shapley",   value: r.shapley_C}
])
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  width: 860, height: 380, marginBottom: 50,
  x: {label: null, tickFormat: d => "I=" + d},
  y: {label: "Contribution (pp of CET1)", grid: true},
  fx: {label: null},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Canonical", "Shapley"], label: "Attribution"},
  marks: [
    Plot.barY(shapLong, {fx: "channel", x: "intensity", y: "value", fill: "rule",
                         dx: 0, sort: {fx: null}}),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Why repo is so large at intensity 0.5
The big repo contribution at I=0.5 is the same **default cliff** seen on the
[Headline results](results.qmd) page: a cluster of large banks tips into default there,
and private repo is just enough to pull it back, so the marginal is huge on the
default-driven wipe-to-zero measure. Above 0.5 those banks default regardless, repo
fades, and central-bank credit takes over — which is why the Shapley reattributes much
of repo's I=0.5 spike to the central-bank channel, and why $\varphi_C$ dominates at
I=0.7–0.9. On the frozen (mark-to-market) measure the spike is far milder; toggle the
measure on the Headline results page to see it.
:::

## Sensitivity sweeps

Each sweep perturbs one friction one-at-a-time and re-measures the channel marginals
Δ_U / Δ_R / Δ_C (percentage points of CET1). Δ_U is flat at zero throughout — the
unsecured market is frozen at these intensities — so what you are watching is the split
between **repo (Δ_R)** and **central-bank credit (Δ_C)**, and whether the total benefit
holds. The vertical dashed line marks the headline calibration.

The key is to read the two stress regimes together: **moderate stress (intensity 0.5)**
and **the tail (intensity 1.0)**. They tell opposite halves of one story.

```{ojs}
freeze   = FileAttachment("../data/sensitivity_freeze.csv").csv({typed: true})
fsa      = FileAttachment("../data/sensitivity_fsa.csv").csv({typed: true})
rho      = FileAttachment("../data/sensitivity_rho.csv").csv({typed: true})
runk1    = FileAttachment("../data/sensitivity_run_k1.csv").csv({typed: true})
freezeT  = FileAttachment("../data/sensitivity_freeze_i1.csv").csv({typed: true})
fsaT     = FileAttachment("../data/sensitivity_fsa_i1.csv").csv({typed: true})
rhoT     = FileAttachment("../data/sensitivity_rho_i1.csv").csv({typed: true})
runk1T   = FileAttachment("../data/sensitivity_run_k1_i1.csv").csv({typed: true})
```

```{ojs}
function sweepPlot(rows, key, label) {
  const long = rows.flatMap(r => [
    {x: r[key], channel: "Δ_R (repo)", value: r.delta_R_pp},
    {x: r[key], channel: "Δ_C (CB credit)", value: r.delta_C_pp}
  ])
  const hx = rows.filter(r => r.headline === true || r.headline === "TRUE").map(r => r[key])
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 420, height: 250, grid: true, marginBottom: 40,
    x: {label: label},
    y: {label: "Marginal (pp of CET1)"},
    color: {legend: true, domain: ["Δ_R (repo)", "Δ_C (CB credit)"], label: "Channel"},
    marks: [
      hx.length ? Plot.ruleX(hx, {stroke: "grey", strokeDasharray: "3,3"}) : null,
      Plot.line(long, {x: "x", y: "value", stroke: "channel", marker: "circle"}),
      Plot.ruleY([0])
    ].filter(Boolean)
  })
}
```

### Moderate stress (intensity 0.5): repo is the workhorse

Here **repo carries the framework** — Δ_R is large and positive, Δ_C hovers near zero.
Repo congestion (bottom-left) barely matters and the freeze threshold (top-left) is
irrelevant once it is loose enough. The one thing that moves the result is **how hard
depositors run** (bottom-right): below a threshold almost nothing is at stake, above it
the benefit switches on — this is the intensity-0.5 default cliff seen on the results
page.

::: {layout-ncol=2}
```{ojs}
sweepPlot(freeze.filter(r => r.nu === 20), "nr", "Repo-freeze threshold")
```

```{ojs}
sweepPlot(fsa, "amp", "Fire-sale amplifier")
```

```{ojs}
sweepPlot(rho, "rho", "Repo-congestion elasticity")
```

```{ojs}
sweepPlot(runk1, "k1", "Depositor-run intensity")
```
:::

### The tail (intensity 1.0): central-bank credit carries it

At full intensity the picture **inverts**: repo is exhausted (Δ_R ≈ 0 everywhere) and
**central-bank credit does essentially all the work** (Δ_C ≈ 6 pp). This holds across
every perturbation — it is completely flat in repo congestion, and robust to the
fire-sale amplifier and the freeze threshold. Only very severe runs move it, and even
then the contribution stays with the central bank. This is the CBCF acting as the
**tail insurer**: the channel of last resort when nothing else is left.

::: {layout-ncol=2}
```{ojs}
sweepPlot(freezeT.filter(r => r.nu === 20), "nr", "Repo-freeze threshold")
```

```{ojs}
sweepPlot(fsaT, "amp", "Fire-sale amplifier")
```

```{ojs}
sweepPlot(rhoT, "rho", "Repo-congestion elasticity")
```

```{ojs}
sweepPlot(runk1T, "k1", "Depositor-run intensity")
```
:::

**Together** the two regimes are the paper's central claim, seen through the robustness
lens: private repo absorbs moderate stress, the central bank absorbs the tail, and this
handoff survives perturbing every friction we vary.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Notes
Shapley values average each channel's marginal over the six activation orderings of
{U, R, C}; standard errors follow by exact propagation from the arm-level cross-seed
errors. Sensitivity sweeps vary one friction at a time, ten seeds per stochastic cell,
measured at intensity 0.5 (moderate) and 1.0 (tail); the freeze panels fix the
unsecured-freeze threshold at its headline value and vary the repo-freeze threshold.
Δ_U is omitted from the panels because it is zero at both intensities (frozen unsecured
market). All aggregates over the whole 67-bank sample.
:::
